blocks.content: {{term:stakeholder|Stakeholder analysis}} identifies all individuals and groups who influence a {{term:six-sigma|Six Sigma}} project or are affected by it, and classifies them by their influence and attitude toward the project. It is a central tool of the Define phase and forms the basis for targeted communication and change management.

A person or group that can either influence the project or is affected by its outcome — e.g. sponsor, operators, customers, IT, works council, sales. Those overlooked may later slow or block progress.
How strongly can this person promote or hinder the project? High power = formal decision authority or informal influence.
How much does the result affect them? High interest = the project outcome directly changes their daily work or goals.

Stakeholders are placed in four quadrants: high/high ("Manage closely"), high/low ("Keep satisfied"), low/high ("Keep informed"), low/low ("Monitor"). Each quadrant calls for a different communication approach.

Where does the stakeholder stand today: supporter, neutral, or critic? The tool records the current attitude. Note under "Expectations / Concerns" where they should stand for the project to succeed and how you will get them there — the gap marks the action need. In the matrix, the dot colour shows the attitude (green supporter, yellow neutral, red critic). If a critic sits in the "Manage Closely" quadrant, the tool shows a warning above the matrix — a key stakeholder must not be against the project.

items: Build the stakeholder list — include all functions and levels the process touches.
Estimate influence and interest for each (e.g. scale 1–5).
Place each stakeholder in the power-interest matrix — every entry gets a quadrant.
Capture the current attitude (critic / neutral / supporter); record the target attitude under "Expectations / Concerns".
Derive a communication strategy per stakeholder — e.g. weekly update, one-on-one talk, workshop participation.
Refresh the list regularly — stakeholders change stance, new ones appear, old ones leave.

blocks.content: Indirectly affected groups (IT, purchasing, compliance) are easy to miss — and later block from the background. When brainstorming, deliberately walk through all interfaces.
Influence is not equal to position. An experienced operator may have more change-making power than a senior manager far from the process. Estimate real impact, not the org chart.
Stakeholders with a negative stance tend to be excluded from the plan. That is dangerous — they need the most attention. Approach them deliberately.
Stakeholder stances change. A matrix built once ages quickly. Refresh at least at every tollgate.
A power-interest matrix with labels like "opponent" does not belong in open project folders. Treat as confidential, otherwise political problems arise.
"We send a regular email" is not a strategy. Per stakeholder, define concretely: what should they know, in which form, how often, who delivers it?
